B05_00: During development, axons that connect the two halves of the nervous system must cross the body midline exactly once, in the spinal cord and hindbrain. This ensures correct left-right wiring of motor and sensory circuits. When it fails, hindbrain axons do not cross, causing horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, in which affected people cannot move their eyes sideways and develop a curved spine.
B05_01: This signal steers both blood vessel growth and nerve wiring, but in opposite directions: in endothelial cells it promotes migration during new vessel formation, while in neurons it makes the tips of growing axons collapse and retract. It therefore shapes vascular patterning and axon guidance during development, with the outcome depending on the cell type that receives it.
B05_02: In the developing brain, growing axons must decide whether to cross the midline, and this scaffolding interaction links guidance receptors at the advancing axon tip to other neuronal signals. It lets neurons integrate guidance information with their broader signalling state while wiring the nervous system. The interaction has been demonstrated in brain tissue, but its physiological consequences remain undefined.
B05_03: This adhesion receptor, found on subsets of neurons and glia, supports neuronal survival, the outgrowth of neuronal processes and the steering of growing axons during wiring of the developing nervous system. Its absence is associated with abnormal axon targeting and neurodevelopmental deficits, and it has been linked to intellectual disability in people with deletions of its chromosomal region.
B05_04: Developing neurons need to advance the tips of their axons and migrate to the right places, which requires gripping the surrounding substrate at the front and releasing it at the back. This recycling of an adhesion molecule supports axon outgrowth and neuronal migration in the developing brain. Mutations in the adhesion molecule cause X-linked hydrocephalus and absence of the corpus callosum.
B05_05: Growing axons of commissural and other projecting neurons are steered away from a guidance cue that elsewhere attracts them, shaping their trajectories through the developing nervous system. The same receptors pattern developing blood vessels and control cell survival, triggering death when unoccupied. Loss of this steering causes misrouted commissures and defective neural wiring.
B05_06: These adhesion receptors on developing neurons guide growing axons and ensure that branches of the same neuron, and neighbouring neurons of the same type, spread out without overlapping. Loss disrupts dendritic tiling and the regular mosaic of retinal neurons, and impairs midline crossing of commissural axons. The gene lies in the chromosome region associated with Down syndrome, though a causal role is unproven.
B05_07: This adhesion receptor helps axons find their targets in the developing nervous system and helps build the specialised gaps in the myelin sheath of nerve fibres, the nodes of Ranvier, where electrical impulses are regenerated. It also contributes to synaptic organisation. It is needed for normal eye development, and its loss is associated with axon guidance errors and lens defects.
B05_08: This anchoring positions adhesion and electrical excitability machinery at specific sites on a neuron's surface, supporting axon guidance, branching and synapse formation of cortical inhibitory neurons and allowing action potentials to start and travel reliably along nerve fibres. Its importance extends to heart and red blood cells: defects cause X-linked hydrocephalus, spastic paraplegia, epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmia and hereditary spherocytosis.
B05_09: Beyond neural wiring, this family of guidance cues tells migrating cells and growing axons where not to go in many tissues. These signals steer axon repulsion and bundling, pattern blood vessel branching, control bone remodelling and modulate the behaviour of B cells and myeloid immune cells. Their loss produces miswired neural circuits, disordered vessel branching and altered immune activation.
B05_10: During development, motor neurons projecting to the head must follow repulsive guidance cues to reach their targets correctly, and this response makes their axons obey those cues. The same response restrains the migration and invasion of other cell types. Loss of this restraint has been linked to increased invasiveness of lung cancer cells, connecting developmental guidance to tumour spread.
B05_11: This adhesion system builds and stabilises the junctions between nerve fibres and the myelinating glial cells that wrap them, including nodes of Ranvier, so that rapid saltatory conduction works. It also contributes to axon targeting, neurite growth and synapse formation in the developing nervous system. Disruption causes conduction failure, and the protein is an autoimmune target in inflammatory demyelinating neuropathies.
B05_12: Pyramidal neurons of the cerebral cortex need richly branched dendrites to receive many synaptic inputs, and this guidance signal, better known for repelling axons, promotes dendritic branching in the developing cortex. Branching sets how cortical circuits are wired. When it is disturbed, neurons develop simplified arbors and altered connectivity of the kind associated with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual disability.
B05_13: Commissural axons in the developing spinal cord are drawn across the midline by an attractive guidance cue, and this response decides whether a growing tip turns toward or away from it, setting long-range wiring. Without it axons fail to reach their targets. Defects in the receptor involved cause congenital mirror movements, where one hand involuntarily copies the other, and agenesis of the corpus callosum.
B05_14: In the developing brain, contact between neighbouring neurons is converted into new synapses as thin protrusions on dendrites mature into stable spines. This process sets synapse density in central nervous system circuits. Without it spines stay immature and synapses sparse, and the same receptors also guide axons and maintain boundaries between tissues elsewhere in the embryo.
B05_15: Growing axons in the peripheral and central nervous systems are repelled by this classic guidance cue, which makes them lose their grip on surrounding tissue and turn away. The same signal restrains migration of non-neuronal cells. Disrupting the response misroutes axons and disturbs the wiring of both the peripheral and central nervous systems during development.
B05_16: This repulsive guidance signal makes cells let go of their surroundings and turn away, shaping axon guidance and the steering of growing nerve tips in the developing nervous system. The same signalling pair is co-opted in blood vessels and tumours, where it influences endothelial behaviour, cancer cell migration and invasive growth, linking neural development to vascular biology and cancer.
B05_17: How strongly a developing neuron responds to midline repulsive cues depends on how much guidance receptor and ligand are present at a given moment, and this regulation sets those levels. It shapes the paths of commissural projections in the developing spinal cord and brain in a cell-type-dependent way. Misregulation contributes to axon guidance defects and to invasive behaviour of cancer cells.
B05_18: When neighbouring cells touch, signals travel in both directions between them, steering growing axons, setting tissue boundaries and shaping dendritic spines in the developing nervous system. Loss of this two-way communication misroutes axons of the corpus callosum and retina. Mutation of one ligand produces craniofrontonasal syndrome, a developmental disorder of the skull and face.
B05_19: In the developing spinal cord, growing axons decide whether to cross the midline, and this response helps set where they advance and where they turn away. Rather than a simple on-off switch, it maintains a set point that also sustains axon outgrowth. Loss of this control produces midline crossing errors and mispatterned commissural tracts linking the two sides of the nervous system.
B05_20: Sensory and cortical axons are kept out of inappropriate territory by a classic repellent cue that makes their growing tips collapse and turn away. This response also helps set the patterns of peripheral nerves and dendrites during development. Without it, axons become insensitive to a major guidance cue and are mistargeted, disturbing the wiring of sensory and central circuits.
B05_21: Contact between neighbouring cells often ends in withdrawal, and this repulsion steers growing axons, axon branches and migrating cells away from inappropriate territory. It patterns topographic visual maps, guides commissural and corticospinal axons and keeps tissue boundaries sharp in the embryo. Its loss produces miswired projections and disordered segregation of cell populations.
B05_22: This neuronal adhesion molecule also acts as a receptor that converts contact with the surroundings into decisions about axon growth, guidance and cell migration in the developing nervous system. It underlies the extension and pathfinding of nerve processes. Loss-of-function mutations cause X-linked hydrocephalus and related syndromes, with defects of the corticospinal tract and corpus callosum.
B05_23: Growing axons retreat from repellent cues, and this response patterns cortical and sensory projections and supports neuronal differentiation in the developing nervous system. The same machinery remains relevant after injury: its activity is a recurring feature of failed regeneration in injured nerves and of neurodegenerative disease, where it contributes to loss of axonal integrity.
B05_24: Growing axons retreat from territories rich in a repulsive cue, and this response gives topographic maps their graded order, such as the projection of the retina onto the superior colliculus of the midbrain. Losing it produces mistargeted projections and disordered visual maps. More generally, it converts contact between cells into directed withdrawal of the axon during development.
B05_25: Commissural axons are attracted across the midline toward a guidance cue, wiring the two halves of the nervous system together. This attraction is essential for building connections between the left and right sides of the brain and spinal cord. Loss of it leaves midline crossing incomplete, as seen in congenital mirror movements and agenesis of the corpus callosum.
B05_26: Growing commissural and cortical axons are steered away from repellent cues, guiding midline crossing decisions and the positioning of neurons as the cerebral cortex develops. This retraction response is essential for correct neural wiring. Disruption of the genes involved is associated with intellectual disability and defective neuronal migration, linking guidance failures to neurodevelopmental disorders.
B05_27: This step determines whether commissural axons cross the midline once or inappropriately recross, ensuring correct left-right wiring of the developing nervous system. The same receptor-kinase axis is reused outside the nervous system, in establishing epithelial cell polarity and in tumour cell migration, connecting developmental wiring to cancer cell behaviour.
